stories.title: The Norse North Atlantic: settlement, retreat and continuity
stories.subtitle: Iceland, Greenland and Newfoundland from around 870 to the Igaliku farm in 1782
stories.description: Follow the North Atlantic settlements, a precisely dated Newfoundland presence, Greenland’s different regional endings and Iceland’s continuing population. Later Inuit and Greenlandic evidence keeps the story of Greenland visible after Norse settlement.

scenes.title: Iceland: settlement begins a longer history
scenes.body: People began settling Iceland around 870, arriving from Norway and Norse communities in the British Isles. Archaeology in Reykjavík gives this broad history a local setting. Iceland’s population continues through the rest of the story, while institutions, beliefs and political authority change.
scenes.note: Around 870 is a regional settlement estimate. The Reykjavík wall’s 871 ± 2 tephra association is a dating constraint, not a four-year building project or an exact first landing.

scenes.title: Households establish farms in Greenland
scenes.body: Norse households from Iceland settled southwestern Greenland around 985–986. The Eastern Settlement grew around southern fjords, including the Qassiarsuk/Brattahlíð area. Livestock keeping, hunting and household work connected these places to a wider North Atlantic world.
scenes.note: The connection joins source and settlement regions. It is not a day-dated itinerary; every farm did not begin in the same year.

scenes.title: Two settlement regions on Greenland’s west coast
scenes.body: By around the turn of the millennium, the Norse settlement landscape included both the southern Eastern Settlement and the Western Settlement in the Nuuk fjords. Their names describe their relationship within Norse Greenland: both were on the island’s west side. Iceland remained inhabited across the ocean.
scenes.note: The Western record begins at the rounded c.1000 anchor for a late-tenth/early-eleventh-century regional phase. It does not date the founding of modern Nuuk.

scenes.title: A precisely dated presence on Newfoundland
scenes.body: At L’Anse aux Meadows, metal-cut wood from three trees fixes Norse activity to 1021. Turf buildings, ironworking debris and woodworking remains describe a small base where people sheltered and repaired boats. The place lies on Newfoundland, across the Strait of Belle Isle from Labrador.
scenes.note: 1021 dates tree cutting. It does not identify the first arrival, final departure, a named saga crew or an exact Greenland-to-Newfoundland sailing track.

scenes.title: Ari records a tradition of earlier Irish Christians
scenes.body: In Íslendingabók, composed around 1122–1133, Ari Þorgilsson described Christians called papar who had lived in Iceland before Norse settlement. He associated them with Ireland and reported their departure. This preserves a medieval tradition about possible earlier religious voyaging.
scenes.note: The displayed date belongs to Ari’s account, written roughly 250 years after settlement. The evidence does not supply a secure monk-arrival date, monastery location or sailing route.

scenes.title: The Western Settlement reaches its approximate end
scenes.body: The Western Settlement was abandoned around the middle of the fourteenth century. Its regional farming history therefore ends earlier than the Eastern Settlement’s. People continued living in Iceland, and Norse farms remained in southern Greenland.
scenes.note: 1350 is an approximate regional abandonment anchor. It does not identify a witnessed last departure, a destination for the residents, or the fate of every individual.

scenes.title: A wedding at Hvalsey
scenes.body: A wedding was held at Hvalsey church on 16 September 1408. This is the last dated event in the surviving written record of medieval Norse Greenland. Archaeological evidence extends Eastern Settlement occupation beyond that written attestation.
scenes.note: The day belongs to the wedding. Treating it as the day the settlement disappeared would confuse the end of a written record with the end of habitation.

scenes.title: The Eastern Settlement reaches its approximate end
scenes.body: The Eastern Settlement was probably abandoned around the middle of the fifteenth century. Its later ending is distinct from the Western Settlement’s earlier retreat. Environmental and economic pressures remain debated, and no single cause explains every farm’s history.
scenes.note: 1450 is an inferred regional display anchor, not an exact final-departure date. The end of Norse settlement did not empty Greenland, and Iceland’s population continues.

scenes.title: Inuit lives after the Norse settlement period
scenes.body: At Qilakitsoq in the Uummannaq area, two graves preserve clothing and personal evidence from eight Inuit people. Dated around 1475, this local evidence belongs to Greenland’s Inuit history after the approximate Norse settlement endings. The island’s human story continues.
scenes.note: The date concerns these burials. It does not date all houses, establish a cause of death or mark an end to Inuit life.

scenes.title: A family renews farming at Igaliku
scenes.body: Tuperna, Anders Olsen and their family established themselves at Igaliku in 1782 after farming at Upernaviarsuk. Their work belongs to Inuit and colonial family history. It was a later development in the southern farming landscape, separated from the medieval Norse settlement period.
scenes.note: This dates a family relocation. It does not establish uninterrupted farming at the same site from the Norse period onward.

scenes.title: A new town in an Indigenous homeland
scenes.body: Ittoqqortoormiit was established at Scoresby Sound in 1925 as settlement policy extended along Greenland’s east coast. Greenlandic settlers built lives around the new town and hunting landscape. The town’s foundation is one event within a much longer Indigenous history of the region.
scenes.note: The 1925 marker dates the modern town, not the first Indigenous presence around Scoresby Sound or an individual family’s voyage.

scenes.title: The timeline ends; communities continue
scenes.body: Iceland remains inhabited at the atlas’s 1934 endpoint. The earlier scenes also show Greenland’s history continuing through Inuit families and later communities after the Norse settlements ended. These are changing societies, not an unchanged Viking culture surviving in place.
scenes.note: 1934 is the atlas coverage limit. The broad Iceland habitation record remains ongoing; Greenland’s selected local dates should not be mistaken for the beginning or end of all community life.
